title: An Indian Sailor Was Killed When Iranian Missiles Hit Two UAE Tankers in the Strait of Hormuz. Six More Indians Were Wounded.
excerpt: The strikes on the Mombasa and Al Bahiyah mark the first confirmed death of an Indian national in direct combat action during the Gulf war. For 90,000 Indian seafarers in the region, the waterway they transit daily has become a battlefield.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • An Indian sailor was killed in missile strikes on UAE tankers in the Strait of Hormuz.
  • Six other Indians were wounded, marking a significant escalation in the Gulf war.
  • India condemned the attacks, emphasizing the need for safe navigation in international waters.
  • The Strait of Hormuz is critical, with 20% of global oil traffic passing through it.
  • Oil prices surged over 9% following the attacks, reflecting market instability.

An Indian crew member was killed and six other Indian nationals were wounded on Monday when Iranian cruise missiles struck two Emirati oil tankers transiting the Strait of Hormuz, the United Arab Emirates Ministry of Defence confirmed. The tankers — the Mombasa and Al Bahiyah — were hit in the southern lane of the strait while sailing through Omani territorial waters, the ministry said. Two Ukrainian nationals were also among the eight wounded. Four of the injured were described as seriously hurt. The dead crew member was aboard the Mombasa. Both vessels caught fire after the strikes, though the UAE said the blazes had been brought under control. ## India Condemns the Escalation India's Ministry of External Affairs had already issued a sharp condemnation on Saturday after the earlier attack on the Cyprus-flagged container ship GFS Galaxy, which left one Indian crew member — a third engineer — still missing. In that statement, spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal described the continuing attacks on commercial shipping as "deeply worrisome." "The targeting of commercial shipping and civilian infrastructure in the region must end, and free and unimpeded navigation and commerce through the region's international waterways, in keeping with international law, must be restored at the earliest," Jaiswal said. The Monday tanker attack marks a significant escalation: it is the first confirmed death of an Indian national in direct combat action during the Gulf war, which began on February 28. ## Iran's Justification Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said it had struck and disabled two "offending" supertankers after they ignored repeated warnings, switched off their navigation systems, and attempted to pass through what the Guards described as a mined route. The IRGC's statement did not name the vessels or confirm whether it was referring to the same tankers identified by the UAE. It accused the United States of "inciting vessels to use an illegal route" and warned that cooperation with the "aggressor enemy" would only worsen the global energy crisis. ## The Human Cost for Indian Seafarers India supplies roughly a quarter of a million active seafarers to the global merchant fleet — more than any other country. According to the International Chamber of Shipping, Indian nationals account for approximately 15 percent of the world's 1.89 million seafarers. The Strait of Hormuz, through which roughly 20 percent of the world's oil and gas traffic passes, has been the most dangerous stretch of water for merchant sailors since the war began. Ship-tracking data from MarineTraffic showed vessel activity through the strait declined by about 52 percent between July 10 and 12 compared to the previous week. On Sunday, only six vessels transited the strait — the lowest in five weeks. For the estimated 90,000 Indian seafarers currently deployed in and around the Gulf, the risks are no longer theoretical. The GFS Galaxy attack on Saturday left 10 of 11 Indian crew members rescued by the Oman Navy, with one still missing. Monday's tanker attack added a confirmed fatality and six wounded to the toll.

## A Blockade Takes Shape The tanker strikes came the same day President Donald Trump announced the reinstatement of the U.S. naval blockade of Iranian shipping and proposed a 20 percent fee on all cargo transiting the strait. The U.S. Navy-led Joint Maritime Information Center said the blockade would take effect at 2000 GMT on Tuesday. Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi responded that Tehran had always been the guardian of the strait and would remain so "forever." The UN's International Maritime Organization pushed back against any toll proposal, saying there is no legal basis for mandatory fees on international straits. Oil prices jumped more than 9 percent on Monday, with Brent crude posting its biggest single-day dollar gain since April 2. Brent settled at $83.30 per barrel. On Tuesday in Asian trading, Brent climbed another 2 percent to $85.50 — its highest since mid-June. ## What This Means for the Diaspora For NRI families with relatives working on ships in the Gulf, the war's toll is now measured in lives, not just oil prices. India's Directorate General of Shipping has issued advisories urging Indian-flagged vessels to avoid the strait where possible, but the geography leaves little room for alternative routes for tankers serving Gulf ports. The National Union of Seafarers of India has called on the government to negotiate safe-passage corridors for commercial vessels carrying Indian crew, similar to the humanitarian corridors established during the Houthi crisis in the Red Sea.

With two attacks on Indian-crewed vessels in three days — one leaving a sailor dead, another leaving one missing — the demand for concrete protection is growing louder.
